title: Powering modern data analytics in Fabric Data Warehouse | OD813

segments.text: MARAKI KETEMA: Hello,
and welcome to the Fabric Data Warehousing session.
We are so excited to tell you all
about the amazing announcements that we have coming to you.
My name is Maraki Ketema, and I'm joined
by my incredible colleagues, Joanna and Rakesh.
We are some of the product leads on this team,
and we've been working hard to deliver amazing innovations
that will make your lives so much easier in this new AI world
that we're all living in.
But before we get started, I want to tell you a little bit
about the Fabric platform.
You've probably seen this slide before, so I won't spend a lot
of time on it, but it's the unified data platform for all
of your AI and BI needs.
Whether you will need to cleanse your data, analyze your data,
understand real-time insights or leverage agentic capabilities,
Microsoft Fabric can serve you with all of those needs.
Fabric data warehousing in particular is
in an ideal position to serve the AI world.
It features a lakehouse architecture
with an open storage format.
It decouples compute and storage.
Storage is bottomless and inexpensive, and you don't need
to create data silos to share data around.
We're also serverless, featuring both hyperscalable,
stateless compute nodes for ultrafast performance
and stateful nodes with local SSD caching for faster insights.
Fabric DW manages your data for you.
You don't have to worry about vacuuming
or optimizing your data, things just happen
under the hood automatically.
And the best part is that Fabric DW borrows its query optimizer
from SQL Server, the best query optimizer on the market,
handling imperfect SQL automatically
so you don't have to worry about it.
And finally, Fabric DW is fully integrated
into the Fabric platform, with a single service layer for all
of your administration, governance, security,
and observability needs.
Our customers love Fabric DW.
Here is a quote from Epic, where they're using Fabric
to transform how they serve their clinicians,
their analysts, everybody within their organization.
Now, if we take a look at the timeline here,
data platforms have evolved in waves.
Early on it was about reporting and dashboards.
Then we moved to large-scale cloud analytics.
What's different now is the shift to AI-driven
and agentic experiences.
You all feel it every day in your everyday work
as you develop applications and run analytics processes.
Now, these experiences are fundamentally changing what
people expect from their data platforms.
Teams are shifting to dynamic and AI-driven interactions.
And it's not just about data or more queries.
The nature of the workload itself is different.
There's a shift towards interactive experiences,
where users expect immediate responses
and continuous iteration.
Now, at the same time, scale
and concurrency are increasing rapidly.
These workloads are coming from applications, agents, reports,
and pipelines, all at the same time.
And this is what's pushing data warehousing to its limits.
And as demand grows, traditional scaling approaches begin
to show diminishing returns.
Teams often compensate through additional capacity planning,
tuning to keep experiences responsive.
But this is not scalable.
So when we step back, what the timeline shows is a clear
inflection point.
Something more is needed to meet your needs
and support AI-driven workloads.
Now, on the Fabric DW team, we took this feedback to heart.
And this is where a fundamentally different approach
is needed.
We built a GPU-accelerated data warehouse in Fabric,
specifically built for the modern AI workloads.
Now, at a high level, what it does is quite simple,
it accelerates analytics and AI workloads
by executing queries directly on GPUs.
What that means is that we process complex
and large-scale queries much more efficiently.
Now, this translates to in practice faster insights
for all of your users.
Whether you're running analytics queries, powering reports,
supporting AI-driven scenarios,
building analytical applications,
your users get results much more quickly and consistently.
At the same time, we made this GPU accelerator data warehouse
super simple to use.
There's no rearchitecting required.
You do not need to rewrite queries
or manage separate systems.
It's designed to be easy and simple to use.
Everything we built, just like everything else in Fabric,
is designed with enterprise scale and reliability in mind.
That means that the system is built to handle high concurrency
and large data volumes,
while maintaining predictable performance at every step.
What's especially exciting is how broadly it applies.
This is not just about improving a single query
or a single workload, this powers agents, applications,
and reports, all at the same time,
all using the same foundation.
So instead of optimizing as a developer for one scenario
at a time, you now have a unified platform powered
by GPU-accelerated data warehousing
that supports interactive analytics,
AI-driven experiences, and real-time applications
without tradeoffs, without extra knobs and the need to adjust
to meet the needs of today's scale in AI workloads.
Let's jump into it.
So here is how it actually works.
Nothing changes for you.
You continue using existing clients
and standard SQL to issue queries.
These queries flow through the SQL frontend, and they're parsed
and optimized, then they're pushed
into the distribution engine, and that's broken
down into different plans that are executed by the system.
The difference is under the hood.
Instead of relying only on CPUs, queries or portions of queries,
can be pushed down to GPUs.
And this allows each backend
to execute complex operations much more efficiently
on these GPUs.
Now, all of this runs in parallel across nodes and GPUs,
which results in a combined final output and an output
that your users receive faster than ever before.
From a user's perspective, it's the same SQL surface area.
It's the same query that you're writing.
And it's leveraging the same exact architecture with GPUs
on top of it to power your users with faster insights.
Let's jump into the demo
of how this actually works in the product.
I'm a developer building an application on top
of Fabric Data Warehouse,
and I want to make sure my users get insights instantly,
whether they're viewing dashboards or asking questions
of an analytics agent.
Here we are in Fabric DW.
I'm going to go ahead and run a couple of ad hoc queries.
At the bottom, I can quickly tell
that there's a brand new option called "Query Acceleration".
It tells me that it's off, but I can navigate
to "Workspace Settings" and under "Data Warehousing,"
find the "Query Acceleration" option and turn it on.
And once it's on, it's applied to every SQL endpoint
and every data warehouse in this workspace.
Using it is simple, I just hit "Run," and I can see
that my query is being accelerated.
Monitoring gives me visibility
into what was accelerated and what was not.
From this brand new column, I can quickly tell
that several queries have already been accelerated.
Frequently run queries gives me even more visibility,
with a count of the total accelerated runs
for a particular query.
And when I return to the query editor and click
on "Query Acceleration," I'm given a bird's eye view
of the value this capability is adding
for my particular data warehouse.
Roughly 89% of the queries were accelerated, which is huge.
We're super-excited to get this GPU power data warehouse
into your hands and accelerate insights faster
than ever before.
Now that you've seen the demo, let's jump into how developers
like you are actually using Query Acceleration
in Fabric Data Warehouse, this GPU-power thing
that we just talked about.
UNC Health is a healthcare company,
and timely insights really matter to them.
And they've been able to leverage Query Acceleration
to help their clinicians
and leaders access insights much faster.
They're seeing 5x improvements on their query speeds.
And the impact for them is
that they spend less time managing performance
and more time delivering meaningful insights
to their users.
And Benjamin Moore is
yet another customer that's been leveraging Query Acceleration
in Fabric Data Warehouse.
And they've told us that it integrates smoothly
and that they've been able to leverage it
and see noticeable performance improvements
for analytics-heavy workloads
within their Fabric Data Warehouse
and within Fabric as a whole.
And this means faster execution for complex queries.
And their hope is to leverage this capability
for large-scale reporting scenarios
and empower their users with quicker access to insights
and support scalable analytics platforms
to improve decision-making speed,
empowering users better than ever before.
We're super excited to bring this limited preview to you.
GPU-accelerated data warehousing can be in your hands.
You can sign up and get access to build apps and deliver AI
and BI insights faster than ever
with GPU-accelerated data warehousing.
But that's not all we have for you today.
I am super excited to introduce my colleague, Joanna,
who's going to tell you a little bit about all the ways
in which Fabric DW is built for developers.
Joanna?
JOANNA PODGOETSKY: Thank you so much, Maraki.
I am super excited to talk to you today about Fabric DW
and its developer capabilities that we're announcing today.
Now, first one, this one's a bit of a "finally" moment.
We all know customers have been waiting for this
for quite some time, because that's let's be honest,
ALTER COLUMN is pretty much table stakes.
Up until now, making data type changes meant rebuilding tables.
Now you can just alter columns in place, no rewrites,
no disruption, no drama.
It just works.
ALTER TABLE inside a transaction.
Here we're bringing transactional safety
to schema changes.
Today when a customer makes multiple changes to a table,
there's always a risk that something fails halfway through,
leaving things in an inconsistent state.
That's painful to fix.
With explicit transactions,
you can group multiple ALTER TABLE operations together
as a single unit, so everything either succeeds
or nothing succeeds.
If something goes wrong,
all changes are rolled back automatically,
which means no partial updates
and no clean-up work after the fact.
The result is a much safer, more predictable schema evolution,
especially for those more complex changes.
T-SQL in the Fabric warehouse continues to evolve
at a rapid pace, with recent updates introducing fuzzy
string-matching capabilities based on Levenshtein
and Jaro-Winkler algorithms, new string concatenation operations,
additional functions like UNISTR, DATE_BUCKET,
along with new aggregates like ANY_VALUE
that expand expressiveness and analytical power
of the Fabric Warehouse.
Scalar UDFs in Fabric Data Warehouse are evolving
to support richer, more complex business logic,
bringing procedural constructs like loops, multipath execution,
and complex if/then/else branches
into your SQL workflows.
These are built for analytical scenarios
and optimized for scale.
They allow you to write cleaner, reusable logic
without compromising performance.
Super excited about this one, lakehouse table health checks.
One of the biggest challenges that customers report to us is
that when they're using a SQL analytics endpoint
to query their lakehouse data,
their data in their lakehouse isn't always
in an optimal state.
It often requires manual maintenance.
Over time things like small files, fragmentations,
excessive updates and deletes build up,
and then directly impacts query performance.
The problem is when performance slows down,
it's pretty often hard to pinpoint why it happened.
It turns into a vague "something's wrong" situation,
but it's kind of hard to know why.
What we're doing here is we're making it a lot easier
for you to self-diagnose.
We now have an official customer-facing diagnostic tool.
It's a simple store procedure called
"spgettablehealthmetrics".
With a single command, you can quickly check the health
of your tables and understand exactly what went wrong.
It doesn't just tell you that performance is off,
it actually pinpoints the root cause.
Whether it's fragmentation, small files, too many deletes
or delayed checkpoints, you'd get very clear
and actionable insights.
So instead of guessing or manually inspecting,
you immediately know what needs to be fixed.
And it isn't just reactive.
You can plug this into your pipelines.
So table health is continuously monitored,
and maintenance can happen proactively at scale.
The key idea here is simple,
we're tuning performance feels slow --
or rather we're turning performance feels slow
into actionable intelligence, making it much easier
to keep your data optimized and your queries running super-fast.
Now, everybody that's familiar
with the Fabric Data Warehouse knows
that our out-of-the-box retention policy is 30 days.
And this doesn't suit all workloads.
Some customers want a higher retention period,
other customers want a lower retention period,
depending on what their workloads need.
Retention allows you to time travel,
do point-in-time restores, perform table clones
for the data retention history period that you specify.
So today we're announcing the ability to modify
that default configurable retention setting anywhere
from one to 120 days.
This flexibility allows teams to balance operational needs
with storage cost optimization,
ensuring historical data is retained
for only as long as needed.
Now, this feature is a super-exciting one.
It's a real gamechanger for performance.
I want to introduce today to you distributive bitmap filters
and how they help speed up queries.
At a high level, the idea is pretty simply.
We run JOINED especially between large fact tables
and a smaller dimension table,
a lot of reasons the fact table don't actually match anything
useful on the other side.
So we end up scanning and moving a lot of data
that we just don't need.
Distributed Bitmap Filters solve
that problem early in the process.
We take the smaller table, build a compact filter from it,
and then push that filter down to
where the large table is being scanned.
That way, we can quickly eliminate rows
that will never match before we even do the drawing.
How awesome is that?
The benefit is that we reduce how much data we need to move
around the system, and everybody knows that's really expensive,
right?
So less IO, fewer resource requests,
and overall faster query execution.
This is particularly helpful for selective JOINs.
But it also improves performance for GROUP BYs aggregations
where filtering early makes a huge difference.
So if you look at the diagram,
the green represents the rows we keep
and the red are the rows we would normally process
but can now skip.
The key takeaway is that we're doing less work up front,
which leads to faster queries end to end.
This feature is coming soon and we expect it
to drive pretty significant performance gains
to common warehouse workloads.
Beyond scale, we've also reimagined the day-to-day
developer experiences in the SQL editor the small papercuts
that add up over a workday, and we've gone
after them pretty deliberately.
First, the new table overview page.
Today, when developers want to understand a table,
they end up writing throwaway queries like, "Select top 100,"
just to get a feel for the data.
We're adding a rich landing experience,
which gives you everything in one place,
full-column metadata with data types.
Second, we've streamlined query management end to end.
We've add autosave controls, copy queries, import and export
of SQL files, and bulk actions
to manage multiple queries at once.
Whether they're interactive on a single complex query
or maintaining a library of dozens, the editor now keeps
up with how developers actually work.
Third -- and this is the one we're most excited about
and I'm sure you will be as well,
Copilot is now embedded directly in line in the SQL editor.
So if you're stuck on a JOIN, you want to optimize a query,
or need to translate a business question into SQL,
Copilot is right there in your flow.
This is where AI assistance starts to feel
like a true pair program rather than a built-on tool.
The next pillar of this release is integration
with broader Fabric ecosystem.
We've deeply connected the warehouse experience to the rest
of Fabric, which is super exciting.
Start with cross-engine analytics.
We've integrated event house endpoint and notebooks directly
into the warehouse experience.
That means you can run KQL queries
against your warehouse data, but jumping to a Spark Notebook
for heavier transformations and to add assigned workflows,
all from the same editor.
Next, copy job creation is now integrated directly
into the editor.
Now you can kick off ingestion and data movement jobs right
from where you're already working.
On the modeling side, Power BI integration now includes Direct
Lake over OneLake semantic model creation,
right from the warehouse.
You can go from raw tables to a production-ready semantic model
in significantly fewer clicks.
And finally, we're adding support for Fabric ontologies,
letting you define business concepts,
hierarchies in relationships over your warehouse tables.
This turns raw schema into a shared business vocabulary,
which becomes especially powerful
as AI agents start querying your data and need
to understand what things actually mean,
not just what columns exist.
From a single editor, you can analyze, model,
and operationalize your data without breaking flow.
Next up, we have some
of the awesome new enterprise readiness features,
which Rakesh is going to cover.
Over to you, Rakesh.
RAKESH KRISHNAN: Thank you, Joanna.
I'm really excited to talk about a number
of exciting enterprise readiness features.
So first up, one of the most consistent feedback we have
hired from our user community is the experience didn't quite hold
up when you loaded a large warehouse
with thousands of tables.
The object explorer felt a little sluggish.
Expanding nodes took forever.
So we've been hard at work at addressing this,
and we reengineered it from the ground up,
built specifically for scale.
The new updated explorer loads really fast
and stays responsive even on the largest warehouses,
(inaudible) testing that the warehouse containing
over 10,000 objects.
With thousands of tables, views and stored procedures,
we saw almost a 2x improvement in (inaudible) performance.
But we didn't stop at just the explorer.
We also re-abled the results grid from the ground up.
White tables with many columns
and full resources now render in a jiffy.
We added native support for large object types.
So working with (inaudible) binary,
along with column resizing,
you will see a substantially improved rendering performance.
And finally, we are rolling
out an enhanced intelligence version as well.
This means faster suggestions, better context, and awareness
for your schema, and overall improved reliability
for your warehouse experiences.
Now, this is the feature many
of our customers have been eagerly awaiting for,
and the one I'm most excited about.
I'm going to be talking about a set of exciting changes
that are coming to the SQL analytics endpoint.
So first up, we are excited
to announce the public preview of the metadata sync.
As you know, for every lakehouse in Fabric,
there is a SQL analytics endpoint created
that lets you query the data
in Lakehouse using familiar SQL constructs.
Now, historically once the data lands in Lakehouse,
there's been a delay before which you can query.
We've been working hard on a new version
of the metadata sync built
on a completely different architecture
that (inaudible) increases the sync performance,
minimizing data staleness.
Your data, once it lands on the lakehouse, will be available
in seconds, not minutes for query.
We can't wait for you to try this new capability.
So continuing on SQL analytics endpoint improvements,
we're extending one of the most loud capabilities
in the warehouse, time-travel to SQL analytics endpoint.
Now, you can create any data on SQL analytics endpoint exactly
as it looked at any point in the first.
The use cases are the ones that every data team runs into day
to day, audits where you need to prove that numbers --
what the numbers were on a specific date,
pointing to comparisons to see how a metric drifted over time.
(Inaudible) when a downstream report looks wrong and you need
to create it back, all of this
with this feature it eliminates the need for you
to create a snapshot or create a copy of your data
for such critical scenarios.
Now, how far back your data can go is governed
by the return string period that you configure in your lakehouse.
Rounding out the SQL analytics endpoint story for this build,
we are bringing enterprise-grade CI/CD support as well.
This pattern customers have asked for is straightforward.
Treat the CI/CD endpoint like any other piece
of production infrastructure with version control,
code review, and automated deployments.
Today, that end-to-end experience is suboptimal,
and we are closing that gap.
So first you have a git-based version control
for SQL endpoint schema,
represented as DacFX database project.
Your schema lives in your source control,
every change is reviewable,
and your endpoint becomes a version artifact,
like any other.
Second, the integration with Fabric pipelines
for deploying schema changes makes it --
the deployments from dev to test to prod
with minimal manual steps.
And finally, it is natively integrated
with the Fabric CI/CD experience,
and that ensures familiar database DevOps tooling for --
that the enterprise teams already use.
Now, continuing on the theme of the CI/CD, I'm super excited
about this new announcement.
We are adding support for pre- and post- deployments scripts.
When it comes to enterprise CI/CD,
there is prep work you have to do, checking prerequisites,
validating environments,
making sure everything is in the right state.
And there is cleanup afterwards: applying permissions,
configuring settings, running validation checks.
Today, all of those deployments live outside the deployment
cycle and in manual steps.
That's where many releases break.
With the support for pre- and post- deployment scripts,
we're addressing these gaps directly.
This turns warehouse deployments into something repeatable
and low risk, with minimal manual steps.
The full release, the prep, the schema chain,
the cleanup become -- everything ensure
that this becomes one governed artifact.
And these two CI/CD changes are coming soon to all your regions.
And shifting gears quite a bit, one of our biggest priorities is
to enable Enterprise customers
in helping modernize their data stacks.
So getting customers from their existing data warehouse,
all the Fabric is one of our key priorities for us,
and the migration assistant is now generally available,
for a set of enhancements
that will make this journey meaningfully simpler.
First, the live connectivity is now generally available.
The system now connects directly to your source system,
eliminating the need for DACPAC extraction
or any manual prep work.
This removes one of the most common blockers customers are
running into today when it comes to migration.
Another exciting announcement we are having is that we have --
we now support.SQL files as an input,
which is going into public preview.
This is when you have existing script schema definitions
or workloads you want to bring
across without going to a live connection.
Essentially, we support a broad variety of sources now,
whether it's Azure Synapse, SQL Server,
or effectively any T-SQL database as a source.
The same tool covers most
of your enterprise migration scenarios.
The bigger picture is the migration
to Fabric has gotten much easier
with significantly lower barriers.
We are excited for you to try all these features out
and begin your Fabric journey.
Now, the set of enterprise features don't end there.
There are some exciting workload management features that have --
that we are about to announce.
I'm handing it back to Joanna to talk about them.
JOANNA PODGOETSKY: Thank you so much, Rakesh.
So in the Fabric Data Warehouse,
we've had intelligent workload management built
in from the get-go.
The system automatically routes queries based
on what they're doing.
Whether it's running a select query
for your reporting workloads, or ingesting and transforming data,
different workloads don't interfere with one another.
Be default, resources are split evenly between select
and non-select workloads.
But in reality, some environments are heavy
on reporting whilst others are more focused
on ingestion and ETL.
With custom SQL pools, you now have direct control
over that 50/50 split, so you can allocate resources in a way
that better matches how your workloads actually behave.
So for example, if you want to have
that split more skewed towards your reporting workloads,
you can increase the select workload group to 80%,
maybe you only need 20% left over for ingestion.
It's all up to you.
We're evolving our billing model
to more closely match how real data warehouse workloads behave.
We will be moving to a node-based billing model,
so you're billed on the actual compute used
to run your queries.
Billing starts with a one-minute minimum, and then moves
to a per second granularity, which means the larger
and more stable your workloads are,
the more that initial minute gets monetized.
In practice, for the kinds
of long-running analytical queries common
in data warehousing workloads, this results
in much more predictable and efficient usage over time.
Combined with improvements to our computer efficiency,
this model is designed to better align
with steady production-grade workloads.
And importantly, this is just the foundation.
We'll continue to build more efficiencies into the engine,
so over time, your workloads benefit even more
from this model without any changes on your end.
So as your workloads scale and run longer,
this model increasingly works in your favor.
And let's talk about cache cooldown.
Cache cooldown gives you control
over how long your compute stays warm between queries.
By configuring the cooldown window,
you can avoid cold starts
and keep frequently-accessed workloads running
with low latency.
It also lets you balance performance and cost,
especially for bursty or intermittent usage patterns.
And because scaling remains automatic, the system can scale
up or down, based on demand, without manual intervention.
In short, you keep the performance benefits
of warm queries while staying efficient
when workloads are idle.
Really, really exciting stuff.
All right, so if you're excited about getting started,
we've made that really easy for you.
We've pulled together everything you need in one place,
documentation to go deeper, a free trial
so you can jump straight in, and guided learning
if you want a structured path.
If you're more technical, we've got architecture content
to help you understand what's happening under the hood.
And if you want to stay ahead,
you can track what's coming next on the roadmap.
And of course, if you want the highlights
from everything we've just discussed,
we've got the Build roundups ready to go.
So whether you are just starting out or already deep in Fabric,
there's something here to help you take the next step.
Thank you so much.
We hope you enjoyed this session.
